what: Science Applications International Corporation provides technology services to the US government. It builds and runs IT systems, networks and software for the Department of Defense, intelligence agencies and civilian departments, and increasingly does mission engineering and digital modernisation work.
customers: Almost entirely the US federal government: defence agencies, the intelligence community, NASA, and civilian departments, under multi-year contracts won by competitive bidding.
money: IT, engineering and mission support for military and intelligence customers.
Systems and services for federal civilian agencies including NASA and transport and treasury departments.
moat: Security clearances and past performance are the barriers. A contractor needs cleared staff, facilities approved for classified work and a record of delivering similar programmes before it can even bid, which keeps the field to a handful of firms. Contracts run for years and incumbents usually win recompetes, because switching a working system carries risk the agency does not want.
risks: Nine analysts average a $132.56 target against a $143.33 price — about 8% below. Analysts rarely publish targets under the market price, so this is a genuine signal of scepticism.
Revenue has been flat for five years, between $7.3B and $7.7B. This is not a growing business.
Federal budgets are set politically, and the current drive to cut government spending and consolidate contracts is a direct risk to the revenue base.
Margins are thin at about 5%, typical of government services where the customer knows the cost base.
Debt of $2.7B against $182.0M of cash is substantial for a business with this little growth.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $619.0M against a $6.0B market value is a large yield, and the shares trade at about 9.7 times free cash flow.
Contracted backlog gives revenue visibility measured in years, which almost no commercial IT services company has.
Defence modernisation and classified work are among the few parts of federal spending with political support across parties.
The company has been buying back stock steadily, which raises per-share figures on flat revenue.
watch: Book-to-bill — the ratio of new contract awards to revenue recognised. Flat revenue is tolerable if the backlog is being replaced; a book-to-bill below one means the revenue decline is already in the post.
view: Government IT services is a business with excellent visibility and no growth, and the two come from the same source. The visibility is excellent because contracts run for years, incumbents usually win the recompete, and the backlog tells you what next year looks like. The growth is absent because the customer is a government that knows exactly what the work costs, negotiates accordingly, and expands its spending only when politics allows. SAIC’s revenue has sat between $7.3 and $7.7 billion for five years, which is the honest description of the business.

What you get in exchange is cash. Free cash flow of $619 million against a $6.0 billion market value is a 10% yield, and the company has been buying back stock, which turns flat revenue into rising earnings per share. That is a legitimate way to make money and it requires nothing heroic from management. At 9.7 times free cash flow you are not paying for growth that is not there.

The reason to be careful right now is political rather than operational. There is an active drive to cut federal spending and consolidate contracts, and a company whose entire revenue is the US government has no second market to turn to. Defence modernisation and classified work are the parts most likely to be protected, and SAIC is weighted toward them — but ’most likely to be protected’ is not the same as safe, and the thirty percent in civilian agencies is more exposed.

The detail I would weigh heaviest is the nine analysts averaging a target about 8% below the share price. Sell-side analysts are structurally reluctant to publish targets under the market; when they do, something in the modelling is uncomfortable. Combined with flat revenue and $2.7 billion of debt, I would read it as the market having already priced the cash yield and the analysts worrying about what replaces the backlog. Book-to-bill is the number that settles it, and it is reported every quarter.
bull: Defence and classified work keeps its budget, backlog is replaced at or above the revenue run rate, and a 10% free cash flow yield plus buybacks compounds per-share value on flat revenue.
bear: Federal spending cuts and contract consolidation hit a company with no customer other than the US government, book-to-bill falls below one, and the revenue decline starts years before it shows.
